hero.headline: Power Your Home with Wood Gas
hero.subheadline: Gasification turns wood and biomass into clean, usable fuel — right in your backyard. No grid required. No complicated chemistry. Just fire, science, and a little DIY spirit.

intro.heading: Turn Wood into Fuel — It's Simpler Than You Think

body.text: Gasification is the process of converting solid biomass — like wood chips, sawdust, or agricultural waste — into a combustible gas called syngas (or wood gas). That gas can power engines, generators, and heating systems.

People have been doing this for over a century. During World War II, hundreds of thousands of vehicles ran on wood gas when petroleum was scarce. Today, off-grid builders and DIY experimenters are rediscovering this technology — and I find myself fascinated by it.

I haven't built one yet — but I'm working toward it, and this site is where I'm collecting and organizing everything I've learned from research, manuals, and the people who have. A simple design can reportedly be completed in a weekend; a reliable working system typically takes 4–8 weeks of part-time effort according to experienced builders.

benefits.description: Wood gas is carbon-neutral when sourced sustainably. Grow your own fuel on your own land.

benefits.description: Wood gas can significantly cut energy costs using biomass you source or grow yourself. *Estimate assumes low-cost local biomass; actual costs vary by system, labor, and location.

benefits.label: No grid required
benefits.description: Run generators, water pumps, and small engines entirely on biomass. Keep the lights on when the grid goes down.

expectations.heading: What home gasification is actually good for
expectations.intro: From everything I've read and researched, this technology works — but it works best for specific things. Here's an honest look at where it seems to deliver, and where it doesn't.

items.detail: A gasifier running a generator during a grid outage is one of the most practical home applications according to experienced builders. You control the fuel supply, the system is relatively simple, and a few hours of run time covers most emergency needs.
Paired with solar or wind, a gasifier can cover the gaps — cloudy weeks, high-demand periods, winter months. It's a natural complement to intermittent renewables when you have a wood supply.

An updraft gasifier connected to a purpose-built burner is reported to be an excellent, controllable heat source. Simpler than an engine setup, lower maintenance, and effective for workshops and outbuildings.

Building and operating a gasifier teaches thermochemistry, fabrication, fluid dynamics, and engine tuning in a hands-on way. Honestly, this is a big part of why I started this site — the learning value alone is compelling.

Continuous operation means continuous fuel loading, ash removal, filter maintenance, and monitoring. Most home builders report this is unsustainable as a daily routine. Part-time operation is the realistic expectation.

items.use_case: Significant cost savings vs. grid power
items.detail: When you account for equipment cost, maintenance, and your time, the economics are marginal compared to grid electricity. Build this for resilience and independence — not primarily to cut your power bill.

expectations.closing: The builders who seem to get the most from this technology are the ones who go in with realistic expectations: a reliable backup system, a supplemental off-grid power source, or a deeply satisfying build project. That's what I'm trying to help with here.
